interpretation.diagram_classification: cosmological / meteorological diagram: wind rose (wheel of the twelve winds) with a central head
interpretation.interpretation: The diagram is a wind wheel. The circle is divided into twelve radial sectors, each labelled with the name of a wind in red, with a second black name or alternative name beside it. The Latin names read include eurus, euro(nothus), auster, africus, libonotus, lips, favonius, zephyrus, chorus, circius, septentrio, aquilo, boreas, vulturnus, subsolanus and apeliotes. The Latin and Greek names are paired in each sector. The central head in profile is probably a personification of the world, or of the cosmos or the human microcosm, around which the winds are arranged. The twelve knotwork triangles at the rim mark the twelve directions or divisions of the circle. The diagram sets out the winds by their positions around the horizon. It belongs to the tradition of wind diagrams found in medieval natural-science and computus manuscripts, which draw on the classical lists of the winds known through encyclopaedic writers such as Isidore of Seville. Because the wheel is set in a manuscript among other text, it presumably illustrates a passage on the winds or the structure of the world.
interpretation.evidence: The red labels and the black labels in the twelve wedges are almost all wind names (eurus, euro, auster, africus, favonius, zephyrus, chorus, circius, septentrio, aquilo, vulturnus, subsolanus). The black names look like Greek equivalents (apoliotes, euronotus, libonotus, lips, argestes, thrascias, meses, caecias, boreas). The radial lines, the outer circle and the twelve knotwork triangles give a regular wheel layout. Step 1 problems: several readings are uncertain and should be treated with caution, such as "AUſTER", "nonus", "erus", "ayrer ir", "FABO NIUS" and "SERTEN TRIO". The Step 1 sector entries also do not record that the red labels on the rim and the black labels inside belong to the same wind. The head is listed only as "head in profile", and the interpretation as a personification of the world or of man rests on convention and is uncertain. Step 1 entries 42-53 connect the knotwork triangles to the central circle through the radial lines, but the lines more probably divide the sectors than join the triangles to the circle. I did not alter these entries.
